item.title: Feeling Anxious: Do You Need to Set Boundaries With Yourself?
item.description:
Anxiety

Feeling Anxious: Do You Need to Set Boundaries With Yourself?

How to address behaviors that relieve anxiety now but make it worse over time.

Posted November 15, 2026

Key points
  • Understandably, many people want to get rid of their anxiety.
  • The things people do to reduce their anxiety in the short term often makes things worse in the long run.
  • There are steps you can take to set anxiety boundaries and help yourself with future anxiety issues.
Source: Edmond Dantès/Pexels

You often hear about setting boundaries with others, but if you struggle with anxiety issues, how about setting boundaries with yourself?

Understandably, anxious people do all sorts of things to try to feel less anxiety. The problem is that the things that we do to manage anxiety might work in the moment, but can ultimately backfire, and they may cement long-term anxiety. Consider the following examples:

  • Jess has panic disorder and does whatever she can to avoid having a panic attack. Specifically, she avoids situations she associates with panic, such as driving on the freeway, going to the movie theater, and being in crowds. She has noticed that her world continues to get smaller and smaller as time goes on. She also frequently checks her heart rate throughout the day on her watch, as she fears having a heart attack (her primary fear during a panic attack).
  • Miguel has generalized anxiety disorder and is very worried about his finances, among other things. He finds he checks his bank accounts and investments at least twice a day for reassurance that he has enough money. He also finds that he asks his wife for reassurance that everything is going to be OK (about a wide range of his worry topics).
  • Shelly constantly worries about her health and her kids’ health. Whenever she feels a weird bodily sensation, is worried about her kids’ health, or reads about someone having a disease, she immediately turns to AI to ask about the symptom or disease she is worried about.
  • Jay is a self-proclaimed people pleaser and struggles with social anxiety. They often say yes to social activities immediately, but when the time comes, they get anxious about not having anything to say or about people judging them. At the last minute, they frequently make up excuses as to why they can’t meet up.
  • Monica has OCD and is terrified that she will be responsible for something terrible happening. For example, before she goes to sleep, she engages in elaborate checking behaviors, such as checking the locks multiple times (because she often doubts whether she checked them well enough the time before) and checking and rechecking the stove to make sure it is off.

Steps for Setting Boundaries to Reduce Long-Term Anxiety

Here are some steps for helping yourself reduce long-term anxiety.

1. Work on accepting anxiety. Often, for people to reduce their long-term anxiety, they need to accept that they might feel anxious and that they can handle experiencing anxiety. So many people have secondary anxiety, or anxiety about anxiety, which only escalates anxiety and makes everything worse for themselves.

How can you accept anxiety? Even just telling yourself that it’s OK to be anxious, that it’s not the end of the world, that it won’t go on forever, and that you can handle it is a start. Committing to reducing anxiety-driven behaviors is another important step. Also, many people would benefit from accepting that uncertainty is a part of life, and not a sign of something wrong.

2. Assess your anxiety-driven behaviors. To set some anxiety boundaries with yourself, you need to figure out what exactly you are doing. You can ask yourself, if I didn’t have issues with anxiety, what would I be doing differently? What would I be doing? What wouldn’t I be doing? Let’s look at anxiety-driven behaviors of the people mentioned above:

  • Jess: avoidance of situations, heart rate checking.
  • Miguel: checking his finances too much, asking his wife for reassurance.
  • Shelly: going to AI for reassurance about health symptoms.
  • Jay: automatically saying yes to social activities, canceling at last minute.
  • Monica: excessive checking of the locks and stove.

3. Set anxiety boundaries with yourself. After you have identified your anxiety-driven behaviors, the next step is to come up with a plan to start reducing them. Here are some boundaries that the above people could set for themselves:

  • Jess: Come up with an exposure plan in which she gradually reduces avoidance; she could also stop wearing her heart rate monitor.
  • Miguel: Reduce checking his finances by first checking once a day, then every other day, then every few days, and so on, until he reaches a schedule that feels more reasonable and less anxiety-driven (maybe once a week or once a month). He could reduce his requests for reassurance from his wife and ask her to stop giving it to him when he asks.
  • Shelly: Work on reducing going to AI asking about body sensations.
  • Jay: Pause before automatically saying yes to social plans and ask themselves if they really want to go. They could make a pact with themselves that if they say yes, then they need to follow through with commitments.
  • Monica: Work on reducing how often she checks various items in her home.

When You Want to Set Anxiety Boundaries and Can’t Do It Alone

Although in theory it might make sense for, say, Jess, to start confronting the situations she is avoiding, she might need more help with effectively addressing her panic attacks, and might need to see an anxiety specialist. The same is true for the other people listed. If you find that you need more support with setting anxiety boundaries with yourself, it can be helpful to find a therapist who has a specialization in the area you want to address.

To find a therapist, please visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: How “Touch Starvation” Hurts Mental Health—and Sex
item.description:
Sex

How “Touch Starvation” Hurts Mental Health—and Sex

As tech and screen time dominate more of life, touch deprivation has soared.

Posted November 15, 2026

Key points
  • Tech-dominated life has caused epidemic "touch starvation."
  • Robust research shows that gentle touch brings many health and psychological benefits—and enhances lovemaking.
  • Sex therapists say sex involves much more than just intercourse. It's based on gentle, whole-body touch.

Personal computers became appliances in 1977. The internet became a public utility in 1995. The iPhone debuted in 2007. These events meant that life increasingly revolved around screen time, today more than ever.

Tech has replaced a good deal of face-to-face human interaction, causing what some psychologists call “an epidemic of loneliness.” The issue became a public health problem in 2020 when the COVID pandemic enforced extended social isolation to a degree never experienced by those spared solitary confinement. Many studies agree that chronic loneliness aggravates stress, contributes to depression, weakens immunity, dramatically increases risk of heart disease and stroke, and in the elderly, accelerates cognitive decline. But loneliness is only one dimension of the harm inflicted by social isolation. Another is the loss of gentle, affectionate, massage-like touch.

Touch and Sex

Of course, gentle, loving touch is fundamental to partner sex. Some sexologists call sex “whole-body massage that eventually extends to the genitals.”

Gentle touch activates special nerves in the skin, C-tactile fibers, aka CT afferents. When stimulated, these nerves trigger release of three compounds key to erotic pleasure:

  • Oxytocin, known as the “bonding” or “love” hormone.
  • Dopamine, which enhances pleasure.
  • Endorphins, the body’s natural pain relievers.

With touch deprivation, these compounds don’t get released, and people can’t experience their benefits. When infants don’t receive regular loving touch, when they aren’t cuddled, their little bodies may shut down from what pediatricians call “failure to thrive,” a condition that may prove fatal. Beyond infancy, touch starvation isn’t fatal, but it drives some people quietly crazy.

Robust Research

A great deal of research shows the benefits of gentle touch, and by extension, the harm suffered from touch starvation. The largest and most ambitious study was conducted by German and Dutch researchers who reviewed several decades of touch/massage research involving some 13,000 men, women, and children (Packheiser, 2024). Most of the studies compared subjects who received gentle, massage-style touch for around 20 minutes with those who did not. Some compared people who touched things like kittens or stuffed animals with those who did not. Both touch recipients—and providers—experienced what the researchers called “massive” benefits: “The evidence is clear that touch is beneficial across a large number of physical and mental health conditions, for all ages, and for both healthy individuals and those with diagnosed conditions.”

In the studies:

  • Twenty minutes of gentle touch consistently reduced blood levels of the stress hormone, cortisol.
  • In people suffering from Alzheimer’s disease who were agitated and difficult to control, 20 minutes of massage a few times a week calmed them.
  • Gentle touch improved mood in people suffering from a broad array of medical conditions, notably chronic pain and breast cancer.
  • Massage or petting animals improved mood and increased happiness.
  • With daily cuddling, infants born prematurely gained more weight faster and were able to leave pediatric intensive care units sooner.
  • Regular affectionate touch consistently helped relieve anxiety and depression.
  • Massage reduced blood pressure, and hastened recovery from fatigue induced by strenuous exercise.

For all age groups but one, it didn’t matter who administered the massages. The exception was newborns born prematurely. Compared with massages administered by medical personnel, for reasons that remain unclear, those infants benefited more from being touched by their parents.

Massage produced significant benefits for everyone, but the greatest life enhancement accrued to those with diagnosed physical or mental health conditions. The researchers encouraged physicians and mental health professionals to incorporate massage routinely into clinical care.

Vision, hearing, smell, and taste all deteriorate with age. Touch does not. The elderly enjoy as much pleasure from gentle touch as young people.

Attention, Heterosexual Gentlemen

While gentle touch helps everyone, compared with men, women experience greater benefit. So, it should come as no surprise that women crave the gentle touch and massage of erotic foreplay, often a great deal more of it than many men provide.

The word “foreplay" is problematic. It implies things that happen before the main event, intercourse. Actually, gentle, leisurely, playful mutual massage fits neatly into lovemaking not only before intercourse, but also during and after. Many sexologists prefer the term “loveplay.”

If you’re a heterosexual man, you’re likely to enjoy better sex and get better reviews as a lover if you spend at least 20 minutes kissing, hugging, and gently massaging your partner from head to toe first.

Many sex therapists suggest that couples trade foot massages before getting into bed. Foot massage feels marvelous. But in the review of touch, foot massage did not produce the greatest benefits. That distinction went to massage of the face and scalp. Try five to 10 minutes of massage above the shoulders before you touch much below them. If men do this, by the time the action moves south, their bodies are more likely to function as they wish, and their partners are more likely to display the sexual responsiveness men want.

item.title: Are Your Dating Standards Too High?
item.description:
Mating

Are Your Dating Standards Too High?

Here are 10 signs that your dating standards may be too high.

Posted November 15, 2026

Key points
  • While it's important to have at least some standards when it comes to dating, the wrong standards can hurt.
  • Focusing too much on the superficial or things that change with time can be signs of unrealistic standards.
  • Try estimating the chances of actually finding someone who would meet your current standards.
Source: New Africa/Shutterstock

Here's something that you never see on social media: men accusing women of having dating standards that are too high. Yep, that's never happened. Neither has women accusing men of the same. In fact, no one of any gender has ever accused anyone else of such things, right?

Umm, not exactly. Anytime someone posts something about having certain dating requirements—unless it's something irrefutable like "I would like someone human"—it's not too surprising to see responses like "you are being unrealistic," "you are too high-maintenance," "no wonder you are single," or "look at yourself." Then the person may fire back with something like "Well, sorry for having standards," and then back and forth it goes.

The question then is where you fall on the whole "got to have some kind of standards" to "being unrealistic" spectrum. That ranges from people who clearly should lower their standards—because a supermodel may not want to date a guy who spends all his days in pajamas posting about red pills on Reddit—to those who actually should raise their standards. Well, here are some signs that your standards may be too high:

Sign 1: You Focus Way Too Much on Superficial Characteristics

If your standards focus on superficial things like looks, then it could be impeding your looking for a partner. For example, a 2020 survey by Pew Research Center found that 15% of respondents “Definitely/probably would not” date someone of a different race/ethnicity—which could end up ruling out lots of people who could be great fits from personality and values standpoints. The same might happen when you base your standards around hair (beyond asking that it be washed occasionally), clothes (with the possible exception of ruling out those who wear a hazmat suit all the time), and other stuff that in the long run won't matter that much for a relationship.

Sign 2: You Focus on Things That Will Change With Time

Many superficial things like looks, hobbies, and fame can change with time—as could your perception and feelings about them. So, be careful about anchoring your preferences on something that may be fleeting versus enduring—especially since the enduring stuff is what often becomes most endearing.

Sign 3: Your Requirements Are Very Specific and Rigid

Beware of sticking rigidly to any rules such as the so-called "6-6-6 rule" that I detailed before for "A Funny Bone to Pick." If you are completely unwilling to consider anyone who's a bit under any of the sixes—height, salary, or abs—ask yourself why. Otherwise, you could end up like the guy I knew who specified that his wife needed to look a certain way, speak at least five languages, and have certain types of degrees, but kind of neglected putting "kind" and "loyal" on that list. Guess what ended up happening?

Sign 4: Your Standards Are Not Your Own

The "6-6-6 rule" is just one example of a standard that you may have heard from elsewhere and then adopted it without really thinking why. Using standards set by others may make others—like fake friends, advertisers, politicians, and Hollywood execs—happy. But what about you?

Sign 5: Those Close to You Keep Telling You That Your Standards Are Too High

Of course, don't summarily reject all suggestions from others—especially when those who are close to and care about you tell you repeatedly that your standards are too high. That includes your therapist, whom you are presumably paying to care about you.

Sign 6: You've Been on Too Few or Too Many Dates

Another potential sign is when dates for you have been about as rare as Halley's Comet sightings. Sure, there may be legit reasons for your dry spell—such as a lack of singles or diversity around you. But what exactly is keeping you from dating the single Halley, who's already expressed interest in you?

A flip-side of this sign is treating dating like casting calls for the next James Bond or Wonder Woman—where you go through a ton of first looks but very, very few second looks. You may believe that dating is a numbers game in some ways. But too exacting standards may be wasting a number of people's time.

Sign 7: The Math Doesn't Look Promising

Speaking of numbers, how about those social media posts that use census data to calculate the actual chances of meeting someone based on your dating standards? Or calculators like the one from Keeper? These may be rough calculations, but they can show how rough things may be for you—especially when your probabilities of success dip below 1%.

Sign 8: You Haven't Actually Seen What You Want

It's a bad sign if you've never, ever seen anywhere on Earth anything that comes close to what your standards indicate. And someone from Middle Earth, a persona portrayed by some celebrity, or any other fantasy character doesn't count. Reality is a lot messier. So, use the successful pairings around you, instead, to help benchmark what's possible.

Sign 9: What You Want Doesn't Really Match What You Have to Offer

Remember, too, that your standards should be based in part on what you currently offer in return. If you yourself aren't loyal and haven't yet gone through an emotional healing journey, then, maybe, just maybe, you can't expect the same out of others. And remember each demand of yours demands more trade-offs from you. If, for example, you want someone driven to achieve boatloads of money and high social status, expect to play second fiddle to that person—or maybe even third or fourth fiddle.

Sign 10: Your Standards Have Very Little to Do With What Would Match You

Finally, check how well your standards match what truly would be a match for you. Will your criteria help or hurt your chances of finding someone with a personality and core values that fit well with yours? If, for example, a primary interest of yours is finding someone who will be very loyal, then maybe being super rich and having a hot, hot, hot body shouldn't be such absolute criteria. You could remove at least one of the "hots" from there.

Ultimately, it is important to have standards. But they do have to stand—stand the test of time and really stand for who you are. If not, you might end up with someone you simply cannot stand.

item.title: Modernizing Nursery Rhymes for the 21st Century
item.description:
Education

Modernizing Nursery Rhymes for the 21st Century

Leveraging the benefits of nursery rhymes while updating antiquated themes.

Posted November 15, 2026

Key points
  • Nursery rhymes teach language, math, and music skills and can advance social and emotional intelligence.
  • With songs frequently dating to the 16th century, parents today often find the themes to be outdated and dark.
  • Pam Gittleman updates the lyrics of nursery rhymes and touts their numerous benefits for today’s audience.

Back in the 1960s when I was growing up, nursery rhymes were an initial gateway to music for children. Their simple melodies, repeated lyrics, and predictable rhyming schemes gently introduced infants and toddlers to the fundamentals of music. What the words actually meant was of little, if any, concern to us young listeners. But times change and these traditional rhymes fell out of favor.

A passion to renew old standards

Revitalizing these classic verses—by preserving their developmental benefits while modernizing their themes—has become the life's passion of early childhood music educator Pam Gittleman. Raised in a musical family, Gittleman was a talented flutist through her college years. However, she did not plan on a career in music. After earning an MBA in marketing, she spent a decade in the corporate sector at a prominent advertising agency before leaving to raise her family.

Drawing on a desire to work with children, she leveraged her musical background to reinvent herself as a preschool music teacher. Over seven years at a summer day camp, she experimented with various teaching methods for children aged three to five, ultimately designing a curriculum centered on singing, movement, and call-and-response activities. As her own children grew up, she pivoted to teaching at nursery schools during the academic year.

Times change

Nursery Rhymes for Kinder Times® offers books, videos, and music.
Source: Photo rights owned by, and reproduced here with permission of, Pam Gittleman.

Over the years, Gittleman noticed a striking trend: the young children in her classrooms were unfamiliar with the traditional nursery rhymes that prior generations knew by heart. Curious, she questioned parents and fellow educators and discovered that the internet had changed how families vetted content. Today’s parents were consulting childhood development experts and sharing their findings online. Many of them found traditional nursery rhymes to be outdated, dark, and inappropriate for young minds, so they avoided the genre entirely.

While recognizing the validity of these concerns, Gittleman’s professional training and instincts told her that the time-honored nursery rhymes still held value for teaching language skills as well as social and emotional intelligence. To bridge this gap, she began rewriting the lyrics.

Her venture received a major boost in 2020 when she enrolled in the year-long Advanced Leadership Initiative (ALI) at Harvard University. Despite pandemic-related disruptions, she had access to advanced graduate courses in education, thus establishing a firm theoretical foundation for how music and storytelling contribute to social and emotional learning (SEL) in early childhood.

Ways nursery rhymes teach children

Gittleman emphasizes that the linguistic structure of nursery rhymes is vital for early language acquisition. For instance, in the verses of “This old man, he played one, he played knick-knack on my thumb," children begin to learn the concept of rhyming. Educators can then challenge them to find other words that rhyme with "one," effectively expanding their vocabulary. Furthermore, because "one" and "thumb" don’t rhyme strictly speaking, children also learn that the concept of rhyming has flexibility.

Since many nursery rhymes are songs—set in a rhythmic structure and vocalized to musical notes—they stimulate important neurological pathways. Rhythm, for example, is processed simultaneously in the auditory and motor regions of the brain. Nursery rhymes capitalize on this connection, helping children regulate their motor functions through alternating periods of movement and rest. Gittleman notes that mastering this physical self-regulation translates to better behavioral and social functioning with others.1

Nursery rhymes can introduce basic math skills, too. Returning to the example of “This Old Man,” the song helps children learn to count, reaching ever higher numbers as they grow older. The rhymes are also repetitive—as children catch on to patterns, they learn to predict and reproduce them on their own. The excitement and anticipation of what comes next feeds the motivation and reward centers of the brain, allowing young children to experience joy while making music and learning language.

Yet another contribution of nursery rhymes is found in call-and-response verses. The call-and-response structure mirrors conversational patterns, teaching young children the social importance of taking turns.2

Modernizing nursery rhymes

Equipped with decades of classroom experience along with academic knowledge obtained through her program at Harvard, Gittleman has systematically updated classic lyrics to be of service to social and emotional learning.3 Prioritizing kindness, empathy, and gratitude, she transformed "Three Blind Mice" to "Three Kind Mice" and, under her pen, the story of “Humpty Dumpty” has been reimagined so that when he falls off the wall his friends come to his aid, rather than leaving him in pieces on the ground.

Gittleman has since published several volumes of her work under the title Nursery Rhymes for Kinder Times®.4,5 These books feature engaging illustrations for young children and structured text to help growing children develop literacy skills. Pairing each rhyme with emojis and guiding questions, she provides adults with tools to enhance their children’s engagement with the stories while nurturing rich conversations that support emotional intelligence. When she introduced the curriculum to a local preschool, an informal survey of parents and teachers confirmed a positive impact on the children's social and emotional learning.6

Seeking to expand her reach, Gittleman utilized her advertising background to pitch her updated rhymes to the music industry. Her efforts won major support in 2022 when legendary children's performer Raffi—along with his protege, Lindsay Munroe—recorded 15 of her modernized rhymes. Since then, prominent children's recording artist Laurie Berkner has also recorded some of her material.

item.title: Empowering a Competitive Advantage to Optimize Team Play
item.description:
Sport and Competition

Empowering a Competitive Advantage to Optimize Team Play

The 4 core values of a mindset trained by an award-winning basketball coach.

Posted November 15, 2026

Key points
  • Effective mental tools are key to the Miami RedHawks basketball team.
  • This mindset consists of four core values.
  • The coach's approach to mindset training embodies psychological flexibility.
Coach Travis Steele training competitive mindset with his Miami RedHawks basketball team.
Source: Photo provided by the Miami Unioversity Athletic Department.

This post is part two of a series. Read part one here.

Welcome back for a dive into the Miami Mindset, a methodology for shaping a mental approach to competition trained by Travis Steele, the head basketball coach of the Miami RedHawks, a basketball team that has compiled a 36-0 regular-season record, extending back to the 2024-25 season.

These are the four core values of the Miami Mindset:

  1. Compete at every moment.
  2. Carry your brother.
  3. Embody undeniable confidence.
  4. Strive for magis (Latin for “more”)

An explanation of each value follows, shared by Coach Steele in an interview for these two posts.

Compete at Every Moment

“I need guys that live for competition,” explained Steele. “Competition brings out the best in each other. It’s how we practice. It’s how we lift. It’s how we do academics. Every day’s an audition.”

“We always talk about being the hunter, and not the hunted in everything we do, and it starts with having that competitive mindset,” Steele continued. “We recruit guys that have that gene, but we make sure that comes to life with how we do practice. We create a very, very competitive practice structure that makes that come to life.”

Carry Your Brother

“I use those words because I want it to be a family environment and I want these guys to be great teammates both on and off the court,” detailed Steele. “Elite teammates have a common characteristic, amongst them, that they can make (optimize) others around them. ‘One plus one equals three.’ I can make you better than you are by yourself."

“We get to three if we’re truly invested in each other,” Steele shared. “Pushing each other, holding each other accountable. Accountability is a really important piece, being very direct with teammates.”

“We want guys that are giving energy to others,” Steele said. “How do we make this come to life? If a teammate falls down on the floor, everybody on the floor sprints over and picks him up. We acknowledge the passer. The guy that scores the basket is the one that gets all the credit, so we point to the passer, which I think is important to show connectivity. Another way (for brotherhood) is tight huddles during timeouts and stoppage of play.”

A true family!

The John McClendon 2026 NCAA Basketball Coach of the Year, Travis Steele, head coach of the Miami University RedHawks Travis Steeleof the Miami Unive
Source: Photo provided by the Miami University Athletic Department.

Embody Undeniable Confidence

“You’ve got to embrace the process,” Steele explained. “Everybody’s going to go through tough times. Even if you’re a great shooter, you’re going to miss three or four in a row, and the next time you’re open, you’ve got to be able to shoot.”

“We talk a lot about mental toughness,” he said. “We train our guys about how to respond (to adversity) in different ways. ‘What is your response to adversity?’ because we’re all going to face it. It’s a lot easier to talk about it, but you have to apply it. So, we do a lot of adversity training.”

“We coach the response piece to adversity harder than we do our schematic stuff because, ultimately, our team is going to go through tough times in the middle of the game,” shared Steele. “How can we reset our minds back to neutral and be able to continue to do our jobs at a very high level?”

“I put them in adverse situations every day,” he explained. “I want practice to be harder than the game. You have to work on your response to adversity every single day, and that’s been critically important to our success.”

“Embodying undeniable confidence is done by embracing the process and being mentally tough and understand that your response (to adversity) has to be bigger than the event that just happened,” Steele summarized.

Strive for Magis (More)

“We talked about adversity,” said Steele as he introduced this final core value. “Handling prosperity is just as important. Sometimes guys take their foot off the gas pedal when they’ve won 10 games in a row, or maybe the guy’s playing really well for three or four games in a row, and he takes his foot off the pedal. That’s a pattern for a lot of people, and we have to fight that urge.”

He fights that urge with a picture of a guy driving a car from an inside-the-car view. "Fellas," he explains, "the rearview mirror, there’s a reason why they’re so small. All the games that have happened are in the past ... There’s a reason why the front windshield’s so gosh darned big, because we’ve got to keep our eyes forward. We got to learn from the past, but we’ve got to keep our eyes ahead to see what’s in front of us."

One of the players added, “If we’re listening to everybody telling us how good we are, it distracts us from keeping in front of us.”

“That’s what happens if everybody starts listening to all the people around,” Steele elaborated. “They’re telling them how good they are and then you take the foot off the pedal. You gotta keep your eyes forward. Keep your eye on the ball, or you’re going to strike out. Our guys really understood that."

“My job as one of the leaders of the team, along with our captains, is to make sure that if we sense just an ounce of complacency," Steel explained. "We have different things we can do within practice to ratchet it up quick."

“I try to always gauge the temperature of the room,” he continued. “Where’s their mindset at? Before practice I go up to the players, talk to them, look them in the eyes. I may have to make adjustments. I’ve got a few drills that will raise the competitive spirit in the practice."

“I think the 'Strive for Magis' got really tested last year, more than any year,” Steele reflected, "just because of the run we were on, and I give our guys a lot of credit. We had great player leadership, and we did a great job staying focused on the task at hand and through the whole run that we had.”

As NBA legend Michael Jordan shared with golfer Tiger Woods: “No matter how good they say you are, always keep working on your game.”

A Wrap

Those four core values closely parallel an Acceptance and Commitment Training (ACT) concept called psychological flexibility, defined as:

The ability to stay present with difficult circumstances, thoughts, and feelings, without letting them dictate your behavior, so you can respond effectively.

Coach Steele and his Miami RedHawks basketball team have embraced and empowered all that!

item.title: Are Psychological Evaluations Needed for AI Developers?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Are Psychological Evaluations Needed for AI Developers?

Personal Perspective: Many jobs require psychological evaluations—but not in AI.

Posted November 15, 2026

Key points
  • AI companies have warned about the risk of AI going rogue and causing harm to humans.
  • Another potential risk may be mentally unstable AI developers purposefully building harmful AI tools.
  • Occupationally mandated psychological evaluations of AI developers could lower the risk of such a scenario.

On March 24, 2015, a Germanwings pilot with severe mental issues purposefully crashed a passenger plane with 150 people on board in the French Alps, resulting in the tragic deaths of all passengers. This horrible incident highlighted how important it is that people who work in high-risk fields and have a responsibility for the survival of others are mentally stable.

To ensure this, psychological evaluations are occupationally mandated in some jobs (American Psychological Association, 2017). Jobs in which psychological evaluations are common before starting a job in many states of the U.S. include:

  • Police officers.
  • People working in prisons.
  • Firefighters.
  • People working with the FBI.
  • Pilots.
  • Air traffic controllers.
  • People working in nuclear power plants.

Moreover, in some jobs, psychological evaluations may be conducted with people who are already employed if they show signs of impaired mental health or thinking abilities. This includes, for example, physicians and other healthcare workers.

AI developers and mental health

Should people in certain high-risk AI development roles undergo psychological evaluations?

One group of people that does not routinely undergo mental health screenings is programmers involved in the creation of AI. Over the course of the last few weeks, there has been a lot of discussion in the media about the extent to which rogue AI agents may potentially cause harm to humans in the future or even kill all of humanity. While experts debate about whether AI agents turning on humanity is a real risk or not, one potentially more likely risk of AI often gets ignored.

Just like a pilot could cause a plane to crash on purpose, an AI developer could purposefully build AI models that lack the necessary checks and balances to prevent them from hurting humans, or even an AI that exists with the purpose to harm humans, e.g., by performing hacking attacks on critical infrastructure. Thus, AI does not need to turn rogue by itself to harm humans; one developer doing so on purpose could lead to massive economic and personal harm. Since a scenario like this seems more likely to occur in the near future than AI turning rogue by itself, measures to prevent such an incident are needed. Because there are mental health conditions like antisocial personality disorder, which has been linked to violating the rights of other people without feelings of guilt, or dark personality traits such as psychopathy, such a scenario is not entirely unlikely.

Takeaway

I believe occupationally mandated psychological evaluations of AI developers should be considered.

Given that the big AI companies themselves warn about the potential risks of AI, more psychological research is needed into whether severe, untreated mental health conditions in AI developers could lead to the risk of real harm for other human beings. While no one knows how likely catastrophic events akin to the Germanwings airplane catastrophe would be in the field of AI development and what impact they would have, occupationally mandated psychological evaluations of AI developers could help ensure that only mentally stable people are involved in the development of frontier models with the potential to cause real harm to humans. Thus, professional organizations for psychologists, companies that make hiring and employment decisions in relation to the development of AI tools, and government agencies involved in the regulation of tech companies should consider occupationally mandated psychological evaluations of AI developers.

item.title: When the Bully Is an Adult
item.description:
Bullying

When the Bully Is an Adult

How to recognize adult bullies—and how to help.

Posted November 15, 2026

Key points
  • Adults can engage in bullying behavior toward children.
  • It is difficult, but important, to identify and address these behaviors.
  • Education to adults may help to improve awareness of this concern.

Teachers are often underappreciated and underpaid. In high school, I (EB) had the celebrated teacher and author of Angela’s Ashes (1996), Frank McCourt. And he was as good as they say, if not better. He was inspirational, built my confidence, and taught me to read and write in ways I am forever grateful for. I had less famous, but also fantastic, teachers, who inspired me to learn and grow. At the same time, I have had teachers who filled me with dread. I still remember my kindergarten teacher who, among other things, made me stand, as a 4-year-old, so that the other kids could see the “baby” because I briefly put my thumb in my mouth. Many of us harbor fondness for some of our teachers and anger towards the ones who lacked empathy, even if their behavior did not rise to the level of “abuse,” but rather was adult-sized bullying.

Teachers, and other adults in the lives of children, can treat children in ways that are hurtful. Adult observers are often reluctant to see and act on the warning signs, despite the direct and indirect impact on kids. Some of the warning signs include: insulting comments, even when couched in humor, humiliating remarks or directives, making children cry, publicly calling attention to children’s foibles, and being physically aggressive and controlling, even if it isn’t assaultive. If a behavior would be inappropriate when directed to another adult, it is probably inappropriate when directed toward a child, unless specifically related to normative school-oriented activities. In other words, if an interaction would feel upsetting or humiliating to an adult, it likely would to a child as well. Children may also indicate a problem with a particular adult by telling concerning stories, changing their behavior around the adult, or avoidance of the adult or the activity the adult is involved in.

Adults have more power than children, through their size, their role in the community, and almost every other relevant metric. Because of this power differential, some adults can behave in hurtful ways without realizing the potential impact on children with whom they interact. Why is it that we fail to identify these behaviors as bullying? Some of the reasons include: the privacy inherent in some of these interactions, the wish to avoid confrontation, desire to think the best in other adults, discomfort with the whistleblower role, and self-protection.

Adult bullying in educational settings

Witnesses have to assess whether it is serious enough to have a conversation. When I was a young psychologist, I made extra income by doing psychological testing in a public school. There was a very inappropriate teacher, who anyone, even visiting the school only briefly, could hear yelling and making derogatory comments toward her students. The principal approached me and asked whether I thought there were problems with this teacher. I responded, “Don’t you know?” He nodded. It is hard to take action in such situations, even when it is obvious.

As a psychologist, I continue to hear stories about adult bullying that trouble me. Teachers and other adults in children’s lives are special as they play such a significant role in the lives of the children with whom they interact, most often creating positive experiences. They are afforded status with children which makes the few who are bullies, or otherwise inappropriate, have ample opportunity to use their power to do harm.

What can be done?

  1. Bring the upstander movement to all settings where adults are alone with kids. This would involve educating and empowering adults who observe aggressions and microaggressions to take action. Say something when you notice something inappropriate. Maybe it isn’t a one-time thing.
  2. Reflect on the culture of the observed environment where children are participating. Is it one that encourages genuine and respectful feedback or is it a proverbial soccer field where insults fly from all adults, parents and coaches alike? Is there a culture of responsibility in which adults address issues as they arise or are the observers complacent about these behaviors? Think about what can be done to improve that culture and norms around these behaviors.
  3. Provide more education to kids about the kinds of things that are worthy to tell parents or other adults. Children may hear that they will be in trouble with their parents if they tell, reducing children's reporting and protecting adults from scrutiny.
  4. Educate parents to "drop in" unexpectedly to all environments where their kids are cared for alone by adults.
  5. Provide more education, to all adults working with children, about microaggressions, sarcasm, and poorly disguised anger, and avoiding them. I think one of my daughter’s middle school teachers really believed it when she said kids like sarcasm directed to them. Hint: Nobody likes to have sarcasm directed towards them, and certainly not when the person delivering it has power over them. Sarcasm is different from humor and well-placed irreverence.
  6. Avoid the witch hunt. One wrong move is unlikely to make a big impact. Adults, like all humans, can have a bad day. The patterns matter. Discern whether this is a singular minor misstep or an egregious incident or pattern that needs to be addressed. With constructive feedback, adults can recognize and change their behavior.
  7. Remember all of the kindnesses that teachers and other adults have extended towards children around you. They make a big difference too. Remember the person who made the world a little better through kindness, not only the one who made that negative childhood memory.
